body: English-speaking Canada uses British English spelling and mostly the metric system, measuring speed in kilometres per hour, unlike the US which uses American English and imperial units.
Canada has considerable Generation 2 coverage in rural or remote areas, recognizable by a large circular blur and halo color distortion in the sky, which is rare in the US.
Canada also has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, with a camera mounted lower than regular Gen 4 and a big circular blur with a small front protrusion often including a right-side mirror.
Canada uniquely uses diamond-shaped T-Intersection signs, unlike the US which uses rectangular ones.
Canadian speed signs use the word ‘maximum’ instead of ‘speed limit’, showing higher numbers due to km/h units; US signs use ‘speed limit’ and often end with 5.
Canadian roads mostly have single yellow center lines, though double yellow lines exist and are more common in the US.
Communal mailboxes appear occasionally in Canada, marked sometimes with a red Canada Post logo; personal mailboxes remain common.
Canadian road signs tend to be less wordy than their US counterparts, often omitting written words like ‘railroad crossing’ or ‘yield’.
Each Canadian province has unique licence plates, some more recognizable even when blurred; some provinces do not require front plates.
French is the majority language in Québec and parts of New Brunswick, with bilingual signs common nationally.
Provinces have their own highway shields; the green Trans-Canada Highway shield is found across all provinces.
Unique kilometre markers vary by province; for example, Ontario markers have a white square bottom.
Some provinces have distinct speed limit signs, like Ontario’s with a black bottom and ‘km/h’ text, and Québec’s may include French.
Alberta's black and white cylindrical bollards with two black bands are common at intersections, sometimes with yellow, blue, or green bands.
Manitoba bollards are black and grey, often with an orange stripe. Rectangular wooden versions appear further north.
British Columbia has black-and-white thin, curved bollards, mostly on Vancouver Island, distinguishable from Alberta bollards by shape and band spacing.
Québec’s bollards are long, thin white poles with red or green reflectors on top, always attached to guardrails.
Yellow fire hydrant markers atop signposts are common in Québec; colours differ regionally, with some overlap in New Brunswick.
Rectangular road markers in Québec vary in colour and are occasionally seen in New Brunswick urban areas.
Ontario uses diamond-shaped road markers with varying colours.
Ontario guardrails use cylindrical wooden posts and three metal wires; some posts have reflective white bands.
New Brunswick’s yellow flat bollards are found on the Trans-Canada Highway.
Northwest Territories’ bollard is cylindrical with two thick black bands, similar but distinguishable from Alberta’s thinner-banded bollards.
Pole transformers face the road in British Columbia and New Brunswick but run parallel to wires in other provinces.
In Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, transformers are mounted at a 45-degree angle; PEI poles often feature red numbers.
Distinctive Ontario pole tops have two side insulators and one on top, sometimes stacked, occasionally appearing in other provinces.
Québec poles sometimes have recognizable pole tops with slightly upward-angled insulator rods.
Québec poles sometimes have a vertical black and yellow label with a small 'Q' in the black portion.
Prince Edward Island poles usually have a small white sticker.
Saskatchewan features alternating pole top insulators with one and two insulators switching sides on adjacent poles.
Québec’s T-Intersection signs do not have a checkerboard pattern.
Newfoundland’s T-Intersection signs have a rectangular yellow border around the diamond shape.
British Columbia road signs may have green backsides, also common on Prince Edward Island.
British Columbia uses unique hanging signposts with signs suspended from above.
British Columbia mostly uses concrete barriers instead of traditional guardrails.
In Manitoba, signposts sometimes feature a green and white striped sticker.
Saskatchewan signposts may have white triangles, with varying numbers.
In Saskatchewan, there are sometimes white dashes between yellow centre lines.
Stop signs with ‘Arrêt’ are unique to Québec.
Stop signs showing both ‘Stop’ and ‘Arrêt’ are mostly found in New Brunswick.
Alberta rural roads use a sequential numbering system with Township roads east-west and Range roads north-south.
Alberta has guardrails with small poles connected by three or four metal wires on major highways.
Newfoundland and Labrador wooden guardrail posts usually have pyramid-shaped tops, also seen on some standalone posts.
Fire hydrants in Newfoundland often have a distinctive diamond-shaped marker.
Wooden boxes supporting signs are commonly seen in Newfoundland and Labrador.
Ontario uses orange and black striped traffic cones, whereas Québec uses orange and white striped cones.
Québec exclusively uses red and white chevrons; other provinces use yellow and black ones.
New Brunswick and Nova Scotia often have rectangular lamp heads.
Western Canada is very mountainous, with highest peaks in British Columbia, western Alberta, and Yukon.
Yukon has a boreal, hilly landscape with coniferous trees thinning further north; Generation 2 coverage remains common.
Southern British Columbia’s interior, around Kamloops and Kelowna, is hilly and arid with brown grasslands and pine forests.
The Great Plains are mostly flat with rolling hills, sparse trees, extensive agriculture, and becoming drier near the US border.
Canola fields with bright yellow flowers are mainly found in central southern prairies.
Rouyn-Noranda in northwest Québec has a north-south grid and a gently hilly landscape with agricultural fields and short trees.
Southern Saskatchewan features hilly river valleys, unlike the flatter Great Plains.
Aspen trees with white trunks are common in Manitoba; they turn bright yellow in fall.
The Canadian Shield features exposed rocks across eastern Canada.
The Québec City-Windsor Corridor is Canada’s most densely populated region, mostly flat, green, and agricultural.
Prince Edward Island has red-tinted soil and common potato farming.
Balsam Fir trees with Christmas-tree appearance are common in Newfoundland.
Canadian phone numbers start with a three-digit area code, used for both landline and mobile phones.
Learning provincial flags, especially Québec’s Fleurdelisé, is valuable as they appear frequently.
Newfoundland driveways often feature wooden octagonal bins, occasionally seen in other provinces.
Acadia is a French-speaking cultural region in the Maritimes with a distinctive French-style tricolour flag with a yellow star.
The Dempster Highway links Yukon and Northwest Territories with an unpaved road, Generation 2 coverage, dark brown soil, tundra landscape, and short trees.
The Top of the World Highway near Dawson City in Yukon is known for overcast Generation 2 coverage and high mountains.
Motorcyclists may be seen near Beaver Creek, Yukon, just ahead of the Google car.
AB-93 highway runs through Banff and Jasper, known for sharp-peaked mountains and tall, thin trees.
Near Drumheller, Alberta, the landscape has distinct treeless canyon-like rock formations.
The Trans-Labrador Highway features sunny Generation 4 coverage, thin pine trees, and a low sun ambiance.
Inland Gaspé Peninsula roads traverse mountainous, densely forested terrain with frequent overcast coverage.
Cape Breton Highlands in Nova Scotia have unusual elevation and rich forests of broad-leaf and pine trees.
Route 430 in Newfoundland offers remote Generation 3 coverage with coast to the west and mountains to the east.
The town of Stewart, BC near Alaska features Generation 2 coverage with overcast mountains.
Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital, is urban with bilingual turquoise street signs and unique road markers on outskirts.
Churchill, Manitoba, has trekker coverage featuring a thin antenna on the car and unique street signs.
Tulita, Northwest Territories, has a unique Google car and dark soil, with partial or full car blurring and visible antenna.
Sanikiluaq in Hudson Bay has snowmobile coverage, featuring a driver in a dark brown coat, who becomes invisible outside the town.
Inukjuak, northern Québec, features snowmobile coverage with a visible snowmobile but no visible driver.
Grise Fiord, Canada’s northernmost Street View town, is notable for mountains and coastal ice floes.
Resolute, a northern town, has a barren landscape with patches of snow.
Cambridge Bay in Nunavut uniquely has Generation 2 trekker coverage among settlements.
Qikiqtarjuaq showcases distinct mountains and red-tinted soil.
Kangiqsualujjuaq, northern Québec, is surrounded by green rocky hills with distant trees.
Nain, Labrador coast, has colorful wooden houses, a big hill to the north, and rocky cliffs to the south.
Red Bay on southern Labrador coast has an always-visible coast, red soil, and mostly white houses.
Canada’s northernmost Street View coverage is on Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, showing a glacier in a rocky, barren landscape with no vegetation.
